lesson_title: Read Any Molecule Like an Address
hook_text: Pentan-2-ol looks like code. It's actually a street address — and you can already read it.
clip_script: Every organic name is secretly a delivery address, and you read it from the back. The ending is the family surname: A-N-E means the alkanes, the plain single-bonded family. A-N-O-L means the alcohols, the family with the O-H group on the gate. A-N-O-I-C acid? That's the carboxylic acids — the smallest one is literally the sting in an ant bite. The middle of the name is the street length: meth is one carbon, eth is two, prop is three, but is four, pent is five. And the numbers are house numbers. So pentan-2-ol is a five-carbon street, alcohol family, O-H living at number two. You just read organic chemistry. Building the molecule takes three passes: lay the carbon spine, attach the group at its number, fill every spare bond with hydrogen. Then run the check that catches almost every error ever made: count to four on every carbon. Carbon has exactly four hands — never five, never three. Find a five-handed carbon and you have found your mistake before anyone else does. Surname, street, house number, four hands. The biggest chemistry topic of the year runs on four moves you now own.
visual_style: A chemical name unfolding into a literal street: the suffix becomes a family crest on a gate, five carbon atoms line up as numbered houses, and a cartoon carbon with four arms shakes hands with its neighbours.
mood: Light and empowering — a secret code cracked in sixty seconds.
pacing: Three quick reveals for the three name parts, a steady build sequence, punchy four-hands finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any structure in your exams like an address book.
